name: Paul Roiter
body:
Before Xelix, Nick and I built a peer-to-peer ticketing app called Dingo. 

The idea was simple: let people resell tickets at or below face value instead of through a scalper. We got press coverage, a spot in the Evening Standard, a mention in TechCrunch, and for about 6 months it felt like we'd found something worthy.

The unit economics never worked. Every ticket we processed cost us more to move through the platform than the platform actually made back, and no amount of press coverage fixes a business where the core transaction loses money. 

We shut it down in 2015, quietly, without a press release this time.

What that failure taught me had nothing to do with tickets. It was that a good story and a working business are two completely separate things, and it's dangerously easy to confuse the first for evidence of the second when journalists are calling and the app is climbing download charts. 

I spent the next few years doing investment analysis at Velos Partners specifically because I wanted to get better at telling the difference before I built anything else, looking at other people's businesses and asking the boring, unglamorous question: does the actual transaction make money, not does the story sound good.

When Phil and I started Xelix in 2018, the first thing we did was sitting with a spreadsheet and forcing ourselves to answer, in plain numbers, what a customer would actually pay for and whether we could deliver it for less than that. 

It's a less exciting way to start a company than a TechCrunch mention. It's also the reason Xelix is still here and Dingo isn't.

name: Paul Roiter
body:
I've now had the same conversation with 100s of finance leaders over seven years, and there's a pattern in how Accounts Payable gets treated that I don't think gets said plainly enough: AP is almost never a priority until the exact moment it becomes an emergency.

A duplicate payment goes out. A vendor statement reveals thousands of dollars of missed credit notes. A fraud attempt nearly clears because nobody caught the change in bank details. 

Only then does a CFO ask why nobody was watching this closely enough, and the honest answer is usually that AP was never resourced to watch closely in the first place. It's treated as a processing function - right up until the moment a control failure costs money.

The number that still surprises finance leaders when I share it: our Financial Leakage Report puts the AP opportunity at around $53 billion, duplicates, invoice errors, missed credit notes, and fraud quietly draining value from finance teams who genuinely believe their existing controls have this covered. 

Most of them don't find out how much is actually leaking until they run a proper audit against their transaction data, instead of assuming their ERP's built-in duplicate check is already doing the job.

What has changed the conversation more than any pitch we've ever built is showing finance leaders their own leakage number before they sign anything. 

Nobody argues with their own data the way they'll argue with a vendor's general claim about industry averages. 

The moment AP stops being an abstract cost center and starts being a specific, provable number sitting on their own books, the conversation about priorities changes on its own.

name: Paul Roiter
body:
I get asked constantly, usually by someone slightly nervous about the answer, whether AI is going to replace Accounts Payable teams. 

My honest answer disappoints people looking for a dramatic prediction either way. 

But here's my take:

The manual, repetitive parts of AP, matching invoices to POs, chasing a vendor for a missing statement, flagging a duplicate that a human reviewer would catch eventually anyway, are genuinely well suited to automation, and we've built a business on specific that premise. 

What's harder to automate, and what I don't think gets enough credit in the doom-and-boom takes about AI replacing finance, is judgment: deciding whether an unusual payment pattern is actually fraud or just an unusual but legitimate business reason, deciding how hard to push a vendor relationship over a disputed statement, deciding which control gap is actually worth fixing this quarter versus next year.

What I've watched happen at our best customers is the same people spending their time on that judgment work instead of the repetitive matching that used to consume most of their week. The AP manager who used to spend three days a month manually reconciling statements now spends that time investigating the patterns the reconciliation surfaces, which is a meaningfully different, more valuable job than the one they had before - not a smaller version of it.

I'd rather be honest that this transition is genuinely uneven across companies right now than pretend every finance team is there. Some are still fighting to get basic automation approved internally. But the direction is clear enough, after seven years watching this up close, that I'm comfortable saying the fear of AI replacing the AP function is aimed at the wrong target. The function isn't disappearing. The repetitive half of it is, and what's left is considerably more interesting work for the people doing it.

name: Alisa McPhail
body:
I joined Xelix in 2019 as its first dedicated marketing hire, when the company was 8 people. I grew that function, built the brand, put a proper tech stack in place, and helped take the company from Seed through Series A. 

In 2022, I left for a global marketing role.

A few months later I was back at Xelix, this time as Head of Marketing - joining a company that had grown considerably in my absence and needed the function rebuilt again for a completely different stage of the business. 

Going from 8 people to 40 is a different marketing problem than scaling a marketing team that already exists but needs a sharper strategy and a bigger remit. I'd solved the first problem once already. The second one required different instincts/direction.

What surprised me most, coming back, was how much of the original brand and positioning work had actually held up. 

The team had grown, the product had matured considerably, but the core story we'd built years earlier about what Xelix actually does for a finance team was still recognisably the same one, just told with more proof behind it. 

That continuity told me the early positioning was grounded in what the product genuinely solved rather than a story we'd have to quietly walk back later.

I now sit on the leadership team, own the marketing strategy and revenue targets, and the team has grown from significantly.

The lesson from having built this twice is that a marketing function's second build is rarely a repeat of the first. The company's changed, the stakes are higher, and the version of you doing the rebuilding needs to have actually changed too, or you'll solve this year's problem with last decade's playbook.

name: Alisa McPhail
body:
When people ask what I measure as Head of Marketing at a B2B SaaS scale-up, they usually expect me to lead with impressions or website traffic. 

My actual north star is ARR. Everything else, cost per lead, cost per opportunity, CAC, win rate, pipeline value, team NPS, exists to explain movement in that one number, not to stand on its own as a success metric.

That ordering changes what gets prioritised day to day in ways that aren't always obvious from outside the function. A campaign that generates a lot of leads at a low cost per lead looks great on a dashboard built around lead volume. It looks considerably less great once you trace those leads through to actual pipeline and find that the volume came from a segment that almost never converts into revenue we can retain. 

I've killed campaigns that were, by conventional lead-gen metrics, performing well, because tracing them back to ARR told a different story than the dashboard did on its own.

Running marketing across events, ops, content, product marketing, digital, demand gen, brand, customer marketing, and community, the ARR discipline is what keeps all of those workstreams pointed at the same outcome instead of nine teams individually optimising nine different local metrics. 

A community initiative that builds genuine loyalty but never shows up anywhere near revenue eventually gets questioned the same way an underperforming paid campaign would, regardless of how good it feels internally.

It's a less comfortable way to run marketing than optimising for metrics that are easier to move and easier to feel good about in a monthly report. 

It's also the only way I've found to keep a marketing function honestly accountable to the business it's actually meant to serve, rather than to its own internal sense of activity.

name: Robert Bergs
body:
I joined as a software developer in 2019, back when Xelix was a small team still figuring out what the product actually was. I'm now VP of Engineering, and the job has changed more times than I expected it would.

Not because the mission/direction shifted, but because the size of the team kept forcing the actual job description to change underneath me.

As an individual developer, the job was writing Python, Django, React, shipping features against a roadmap someone else had mostly already scoped. 

As the team grew, the job became less about the code I personally wrote and more about the code the team wrote well together, which meant learning to give up direct control over decisions I used to make alone, on a timeline I could no longer fully predict, because now other people's judgment was part of the process.

The hardest was accepting that a decision made by someone else on the team, one I might have made differently myself, wasn't automatically a mistake just because it wasn't the choice I'd have picked. 

Early on I caught myself quietly rewriting things after review instead of actually having the harder conversation about why I disagreed, which taught the team the wrong lesson: that my review was the real gate, regardless of what got said out loud in the process.

I still contribute code occasionally because staying close enough to the actual codebase to have an opinion about it matters more to me than the title implies it should. 

6 years in, the thing that's stayed constant is a fairly stubborn belief that engineering leadership means making the team better at building this, not making myself the best individual builder in the room.

More to build.

name: Robert Bergs
body:
A big part of what our engineering team builds is systems that decide whether two things - (i) an invoice and a purchase order, or (ii) a payment and a previous payment - are actually the same transaction described slightly differently across two different systems. 

That sounds like a simple matching problem until you've actually tried to build one that holds up against enterprise data.

The naive version of this problem assumes clean, consistent data: the same vendor name spelled the same way, the same invoice number format, amounts that match exactly. 

But enterprise finance data almost never looks like that. 

- The same vendor shows up under three slightly different names across different systems. 
- Amounts differ by small currency conversion rounding. 
- Invoice numbers get manually re-entered with a transposed digit somewhere along the way. 

Building a matching system that's useful means building one that's deliberately tolerant of that mess, without becoming so tolerant it starts flagging genuinely different transactions as duplicates.

That tolerance has to be tuned differently for every customer, because every finance team's actual data mess looks slightly different depending on their ERP setup, their vendor master data hygiene, and how many acquisitions they've been through without ever properly consolidating vendor records afterward. 

At Xelix - we've built our systems specifically to learn that tolerance per customer rather than applying one fixed rule globally, because a rule tight enough to work cleanly for one customer's data would miss duplicates for another customer whose data is messier in different specific ways.

The actual engineering challenge underneath all of this is a well-understood problem. 

It's building a system honest enough to flag its own uncertainty when a match is genuinely ambiguous, rather than forcing a confident yes or no on a case that a human reviewer should actually be looking at directly.

name: Robert Bergs
body:
A lot of conversations about engineering culture default to talking about perks, remote flexibility, learning budgets, the things that show up on a careers page. 

Those matter, and we offer real versions of most of them. None of them are actually what determines whether engineers stay somewhere and do their best work.

What actually determines that, in my experience running an engineering team for years now, is whether an engineer's honest technical disagreement with a decision gets a hearing before the decision gets made.

Engineers can tell the difference between genuine input and a process that performs consultation while the actual call was made somewhere else already. 

The second version erodes trust faster than almost anything else I've watched happen on a team - faster than a missed deadline, faster than a tool they don't like.

Building that input into how decisions actually get made is slower than just deciding things at the top and communicating them clearly afterward. 

- It means sitting with real disagreement in a planning conversation rather than moving past it quickly to protect the timeline. 
- It means occasionally changing a decision because an engineer closer to the actual problem than I am made a better case than my own instinct did.

I'd rather run engineering that way - slower in the room and faster in the execution because people believe in the direction, than one that moves quickly through decisions and slowly through the quiet resentment that follows when people feel like input was theater. 

The perks are the easy part to get right. This part takes actual, ongoing effort, and it never fully stays solved once and for all.

name: Paul Solomon
body:
Before I worked in Accounts Payable, I spent several years using machine learning in sports business advisory. 

I helped clubs, federations, and sponsors understand performance and audience data so they could make better decisions. Before that, I worked at a strategy consulting firm, where I built quantitative models for blue-chip clients. 

At first, moving to lead AI engineering at a finance SaaS company may seem like three very different careers.

However, one important skill stayed the same across all three roles. It was learning how to build a model that helps a decision-maker. 

Most decision-makers do not care about the model itself. They only care if the decision it supports turns out to be correct. 

- A sports federation does not care if your clustering approach is elegant. They care if the sponsorship recommendation actually performs well. 
- A finance leader does not care about our transformer architecture. They care if the fraud flag really identifies fraud.

This is a more difficult standard because a model can have very high technical quality but still not be the most useful in practice. Sometimes, the best technical solution is not the best business solution. You have to be honest about which one you are trying to improve when they lead to different results. 

I have built models that were more advanced technically than the ones we finally used, but we still shipped the simpler version because it was more reliable for the specific decision a finance team needed to make.

My 6 years at Aviva, building ML data products, taught me to ask whether a model is useful before asking whether it is elegant. 

Today, while leading AI engineering at Xelix and working with gradient-boosted trees, fine-tuned transformers, and cloud-hosted LLMs, that is still the first question I ask whenever my team builds something new, even if the more advanced technical solution would be more interesting to create.

name: Paul Solomon
body:
There is a common idea in AI engineering today that the newest LLM should be the first choice for almost every problem. This makes sense because these models are very powerful. However, not every problem needs an LLM. Some tasks can be solved more reliably and at a much lower cost with a gradient-boosted tree.

While leading AI engineering for a production finance platform, I have had to avoid using an LLM as the default solution many times.

For example, detecting whether an invoice is a likely duplicate is mainly a structured, numerical pattern-matching problem. The model checks things like the amount, vendor, date proximity, and invoice number similarity. A well-tuned gradient-boosted model can do this accurately, quickly, and at a much lower cost than sending every invoice to an LLM.

An LLM is more useful for different kinds of tasks. It can understand an unstructured vendor query written in natural language. It can also read a supplier statement that comes as a messy PDF with no consistent format. These tasks involve language and uncertainty, and they are the kinds of problems that structured models were not designed to solve.

The most important architecture decision is choosing the right tool for the right part of the problem instead of always using the tool that is getting the most attention. This idea guides everything we build.

This may not sound as exciting as saying, "We built everything with the latest model." However, it is the reason our systems work reliably and stay affordable, even when our enterprise customers process a very large number of transactions.

Some people may think this explanation makes AI seem less important. It does not. It simply explains which type of AI is doing each job. A fraud-detection classifier and a document-parsing language model are built for different tasks. Treating them as if they are the same can make teams spend more on infrastructure when a simpler and cheaper model could have done the job just as well.

name: Sam Dhingra
body:
I spent 9 years at HighRadius, starting as a Solution Principal in Hyderabad and later becoming Associate Vice President of Solution Engineering in London.

Many people think staying at one company for so long means a person is not ambitious. My experience was different.

I stayed because my role kept changing. I worked in different markets, different countries, and took on bigger responsibilities. As a Solution Principal in India, I learned how to explain complex finance software to customers. Later, in London, I learned how to lead Solution Engineering teams and help others build the same skills.

One important lesson I learned is that changing companies often is not the only way to grow. Moving every few years may help you get a new title, but staying in one place can help you build deeper knowledge of a market, a product, and your customers.

I eventually joined Xelix because it offered a new challenge. It gave me the chance to help build the gtm strategy at an earlier-stage company from a more senior role.

The lesson, however, was not to stay at one company forever, but to move when the role stopped helping you grow, not simply because a certain amount of time had passed.

name: Sam Dhingra
body:
Leading global sales at Xelix, I spend most of my time talking with finance leaders who are naturally skeptical of software vendors. Many have seen promises of transformation but received only small improvements.

Selling to these customers requires a different approach.

Many sales conversations start by talking about a better future and the long-term benefits. But experienced finance leaders have heard these messages many times before.

What gets their attention is showing real evidence from their own business. For example, we can show:

* a real leakage number
* a real duplicate payment rate

These numbers come from their own transaction data, not from industry averages.

This changes the whole sales conversation. Instead of asking customers to imagine a better future, we show them a real problem that already exists in their current process. When customers see the data for themselves, the evidence becomes more convincing than the sales pitch.

My technical background, with an engineering and biological science degree before an MBA in marketing, helps a lot.

It allows me to explain how the matching and detection logic actually works instead of only giving a simple marketing explanation. This helps build trust with technical stakeholders who want to understand the system.

Finance leaders are more likely to trust a vendor when they see that someone on the sales team understands how the technology works, not just how to present it.

name: Sam Dhingra
body:
Most sales training teaches that an objection is something to overcome. Sales reps are often taught to answer the objection quickly and move back to closing the deal.

After leading sales teams across two different companies, I have learned that enterprise finance deals are different.

When a finance stakeholder raises an objection, it is usually not a way to delay the sale. It is a concern from someone whose job is to reduce risk and prevent costly mistakes.

Instead of trying to overcome the objection, I coach reps to see it as the most useful part of the conversation. It helps us understand what the customer is really worried about.

For example, if a finance leader is worried about implementation during a critical close period, we should change the project timeline instead of just saying that onboarding will be smooth.

The deals that have held up best over time, the ones that expand rather than quietly churn a year later, were almost always the ones where we took an early objection seriously enough to actually change something about the proposal, rather than simply talking a stakeholder past their own legitimate hesitation. 

A customer who feels heard trusts the relationship much more than a customer who only feels persuaded.

name: Gwyn Roberts
body:
Across HighRadius, Celonis, Data Interconnect, and BlackLine, I've spent over twenty years selling variations of the same underlying problem: finance teams drowning in manual reconciliation work they don't have the headcount to do properly by hand. Joining Xelix as Head of Enterprise Sales, I'm selling into that same problem again, from a fifth seat, and I've started noticing what actually changes between vendors versus what stays the same regardless of which company's logo is on the deck.

What stays the same is the buyer's actual anxiety. A finance leader evaluating any automation vendor in this space is quietly asking the same question underneath whatever specific pitch they're hearing: will this actually work on our messy, specific data, or will we be the customer whose implementation becomes the cautionary internal story a year from now. That anxiety doesn't change whether the vendor is selling invoice-to-cash, process mining, or accounts payable controls specifically.

What changes, and what I've had to relearn each time I've moved between these companies, is the specific proof that actually addresses that anxiety in each category. In invoice-to-cash at BlackLine, the proof that mattered most was integration depth with existing ERP systems. In process mining at Celonis, it was the specificity of the process bottlenecks the tool could actually surface versus generic dashboards. At Xelix, in accounts payable, the proof that lands hardest is a real leakage number calculated against the prospect's own transaction data, not against an industry benchmark.

Twenty years in, the actual skill I've built isn't a fixed sales methodology that transfers unchanged across every category. It's a faster read on which specific proof point will actually move a skeptical finance buyer in this particular category, this particular quarter, because the underlying anxiety never changes but the evidence that resolves it always does.

name: Gwyn Roberts
body:
I spent the last few years at BlackLine, a large, established public company, before joining Xelix, a Series B business at a considerably earlier stage. The shift wasn't just about company size. It changed nearly everything about how a sales conversation actually gets built and won.

At an established company, a prospect's trust is largely inherited. The brand has been around long enough, has enough existing customers in the prospect's own industry, that a rep spends less time proving the company itself is credible and more time differentiating the specific solution within an already-trusted category. At an earlier-stage company, that inherited trust doesn't exist yet in the same way, and a meaningful part of every conversation is establishing that Xelix itself, not just the product, is a safe, durable bet for a large enterprise to build a critical finance process around.

That's a genuinely different sales skill than the one I'd spent years sharpening at larger, more established vendors. It means leaning harder on specific customer proof, real named enterprise customers, real retention numbers, real implementation timelines, because the company's own maturity can't do that reassurance work on its own the way it could at a twenty-year-old public company.

What's made the adjustment easier than I expected is that Xelix's actual customer roster, global enterprises trusting a critical control function to a Series B company, is itself unusually strong proof for a company at this stage. Most vendors this size don't yet have logos this large trusting them with something this operationally sensitive. Leaning on that specific fact, rather than trying to manufacture the kind of inherited trust a public company has by default, has become the actual foundation of how I sell here now.

name: Gwyn Roberts
body:
There's an assumption in a lot of sales commentary right now that AI-powered tools should be shortening enterprise deal cycles, since buyers can supposedly evaluate faster with better information available to them. My own experience selling enterprise finance software through this exact period has been closer to the opposite.

Enterprise buyers evaluating an AI-powered vendor now ask a meaningfully longer and more specific set of questions than they did evaluating a comparable non-AI tool a few years ago: how is the model trained, what happens when it's wrong, what's the actual human oversight built into the workflow, how is customer data handled inside the model pipeline specifically. Those are legitimate, considered questions from buyers who've read enough about AI risk to be appropriately cautious, and answering them properly takes real time, often involving security and legal stakeholders who weren't part of a comparable evaluation before AI became central to the pitch.

What this has actually meant for enterprise sales in this category is longer cycles with more stakeholders involved earlier, not the faster, more self-serve buying motion the AI hype often implies is coming. I don't think that's a temporary friction that resolves once buyers get more comfortable with AI generally. It's a genuinely new, permanent layer of diligence that a category selling AI into a risk-sensitive function like finance should expect to build into every enterprise deal going forward.

The reps and teams handling this well aren't the ones trying to rush past those questions to protect deal velocity. They're the ones who've built genuinely strong, specific answers to the AI-governance questions before the prospect even asks, treating that diligence as an expected part of the process rather than an unwelcome delay to route around.

name: Chris Nicol
body:
At 15Five, I helped grow the product management function from two people to twelve, ten to fourteen squads over roughly two years, including hiring eight product managers and a CPO along the way. Scaling a product org that fast surfaces problems in a specific, predictable order, and most of them aren't the ones people expect going in.

The first thing that breaks isn't process. It's context. At two people, everyone knows why every decision was made, because they were both in the room for it. By eight or nine people, that shared context quietly stops existing, and decisions that felt obviously correct to the two founding PMs start looking arbitrary to newer hires who never heard the original reasoning. The fix isn't more meetings. It's writing the reasoning down at the moment a decision is made, not after someone asks about it months later.

The second thing that breaks is a founding PM's instinct to still personally review everything, which worked fine at two people and becomes a genuine bottleneck by eight, without most people noticing it's happening because it looks like thoroughness rather than a constraint. I had to consciously build the discipline of trusting a newer PM's call on something I'd have made differently myself, the same discipline I'd later need again leading product at Xelix, just applied to an even larger and more complex team.

What surprised me most, watching this pattern repeat later during the Emplify acquisition and again at Hubble, is how consistent it is across genuinely different products and company cultures. The specific tools and rituals a team adopts differ. The order in which context, then personal review capacity, then simple headcount become the actual bottleneck barely changes at all.

name: Chris Nicol
body:
Alongside leading product at Xelix, I offer career development coaching, mostly to product managers navigating the exact transitions I've been through myself, individual contributor to manager, single-team lead to multi-team leader, operator to someone actually responsible for a P&L-adjacent function. Coaching people through those transitions has taught me something about my own leadership that running my own team never quite surfaced as clearly.

Most of the people I coach aren't stuck because they lack the technical product skill for the next level. They're stuck because the specific behaviors that made them excellent individual contributors, personally owning every important decision, personally reviewing every important artifact, become genuine liabilities the moment they're managing other people doing that same work. Watching this pattern across dozens of coaching conversations, I've started recognizing versions of my own earlier mistakes in almost every session, which is a specific kind of humbling I didn't expect from a coaching role.

The advice I give most often isn't really product advice at all. It's some version of asking a coachee to notice the specific moment they're about to personally fix something a team member got slightly wrong, rather than let the team member's version ship and learn from what happens next. That's a harder discipline than it sounds, because the personal fix genuinely produces a better artifact in the short term, every single time. It just produces a worse team over the long term, one that never fully develops the judgment the leader keeps quietly overriding.

Coaching this in other people has made me considerably more honest with myself about the moments I still catch myself doing exactly this at Xelix, years into leading product here. It's a lesson that apparently has to be relearned at every new scale of responsibility, not one that stays solved once you've genuinely understood it the first time.

name: Chris Nicol
body:
Leading product through the current wave of AI-driven feature development, I've watched a specific failure pattern repeat across our own early attempts and across competitors' products I've evaluated closely: an AI capability gets added to an existing workflow as an extra step, a button a user has to remember to click, rather than being built into the actual flow the user was already in.

Our Helpdesk product's automated reply capability only became genuinely useful once we stopped treating it as a separate AI feature sitting alongside the existing ticket queue and started treating it as the default first step of the queue itself, one the AP team could trust enough not to think about most of the time, only stepping in for the genuinely ambiguous cases. That's a meaningfully different design decision than adding an AI assist button to an otherwise unchanged workflow, and it took us longer to get right than the button version would have.

The pattern I've come to trust now, evaluating any new AI feature before we build it, is asking whether using it requires the user to remember it exists and make an active choice to invoke it, or whether it's genuinely woven into the default path they were already on. Features requiring the first kind of active choice get used enthusiastically for the first week, by early adopters excited about the novelty, and then usage quietly drops off as the excitement fades and the extra step becomes friction nobody wants to keep paying.

The features that hold up, the ones that are still being used just as heavily six months after launch as they were in week one, are almost always the ones woven into a workflow the user never had to consciously choose to adopt in the first place. That's a harder, slower design problem to solve than bolting a new AI button onto an existing screen. It's also the only version I've seen actually stick.

name: Doug Weltman
role: Head of Revenue Operations and Enablement
body:
Between Yahoo and InfoSum, I spent about a year working independently, doing investment analysis and due diligence for venture and growth-stage investors, looking closely at technology entrepreneurs' businesses before anyone wrote a check. It wasn't originally a deliberate career strategy. It was closer to an accident that turned into one of the more useful years of my career.

Spending a year evaluating other people's revenue operations from the outside, rather than building my own inside a company, taught me to spot a specific pattern I now look for constantly: a business whose reported growth looks strong because the underlying unit economics are being subsidized by something temporary, a one-time contract, an unsustainable acquisition channel, a pricing structure the company already knows it will need to change. From inside a company, that subsidy is easy to miss because it's just how things currently are. From outside, doing diligence, it's often the first thing that becomes visible once you actually pull apart the numbers.

That outside vantage point changed how I've approached every revenue operations role since. At InfoSum, building forecasting models and pricing structures, I found myself constantly asking the diligence question I used to ask about other people's companies: if an outside investor looked closely at this specific number, what would they actually find underneath it. That's a genuinely uncomfortable question to keep asking about your own company's numbers, and it's caught real problems earlier than waiting for an actual external diligence process would have.

I don't think every operator needs a formal year outside their own company to build that instinct. I do think deliberately asking the outsider's skeptical question about your own numbers, on a regular schedule rather than only when a fundraise or acquisition forces the question, is the actual habit worth building, and it's the one thing from that in-between year that's stayed with me the longest.

name: Doug Weltman
role: Head of Revenue Operations and Enablement
body:
Most revenue forecasting I've seen across my career produces a single number, a point estimate everyone treats with more confidence than it deserves. At InfoSum, I moved our forecasting to Monte Carlo simulation instead, and I want to explain what that actually means in practice, because it's a genuinely useful shift that gets buried under intimidating-sounding statistical language more often than it needs to be.

Instead of asking the model for one forecasted revenue number, a Monte Carlo approach runs the underlying assumptions, deal probability, average deal size, sales cycle length, thousands of times with slight, randomized variation in each input, and produces a full range of plausible outcomes rather than a single confident guess. The output isn't 'we'll close 4.2 million dollars this quarter.' It's 'there's roughly a seventy percent chance we land between 3.6 and 4.8 million, and a much smaller chance we land outside that range in either direction.'

That range is uncomfortable for a leadership team used to a single confident number, and it's also considerably more honest about what forecasting actually is: an estimate under real uncertainty, not a prediction anyone should stake their planning entirely on as though it were fact. The single-number version feels more decisive in a board meeting. It's also more likely to be quietly, confidently wrong in a way nobody built any contingency around.

What convinced our own leadership team to adopt this approach wasn't the statistical elegance of it. It was watching the range actually predict, correctly, a soft quarter that the old single-point forecast would have called safely on-target right up until it wasn't. Once a forecasting method has correctly flagged risk the simpler method missed, the harder-to-explain version tends to earn its place in the process fairly quickly.

name: Doug Weltman
role: Head of Revenue Operations and Enablement
body:
Revenue operations, in a lot of companies, is treated primarily as a reporting function: build the dashboard, maintain the CRM, produce the forecast. At InfoSum, I pushed our function toward something considerably more hands-on, building actual internal tools, an LLM-based email generation and lead scoring system, an RFP repository with real search functionality, a fuzzy-logic tool for identifying networked selling opportunities across our own customer base.

The case for RevOps building rather than only reporting is straightforward once you sit with it: nobody in the organization understands the actual gaps in the sales and marketing workflow as precisely as the team already responsible for measuring where deals stall and why forecasts miss. A generic off-the-shelf tool solves the generic version of a problem. A tool built by the team that's spent months staring at exactly where your specific pipeline breaks down solves the actual, specific version, and that specificity is usually the entire difference between a tool that gets adopted and one that quietly gets ignored after the initial rollout enthusiasm fades.

Building the RFP search tool specifically came from watching reps waste real hours each week manually searching old documents for a previously-answered security question, a problem visible only to whoever was already tracking rep time allocation closely enough to notice the pattern. A tool built by someone outside RevOps, without that specific visibility, would likely have solved a more generic version of the document search problem instead of the actual, narrower time sink we could see clearly.

I'd rather have a smaller RevOps team that builds a handful of tools solving real, specific gaps than a larger one that only maintains dashboards reporting on problems nobody's actually empowered to fix. The reporting function matters. It shouldn't be the entire job.

name: Jesse Newton
body:
I've been at Xelix nearly four years, through a period of growth from 26 employees to over 160. Owning business operations across people, finance ops, legal ops, and workplace through that stretch taught me a specific lesson about sequencing that I don't think gets discussed enough outside of operations itself: the infrastructure has to exist slightly before the growth that needs it, not slightly after, or the gap between the two becomes genuinely painful to close.

At 26 people, almost nothing needs to be formalized. Everyone knows everyone, decisions get made in conversations, and building a proper HRIS or a formal OKR cadence at that size would be premature process for its own sake. Somewhere between 40 and 60 people, that changes, and it changes faster than most operations functions anticipate, because the signal that you've crossed the threshold isn't a clean number on a headcount chart. It's a specific kind of confusion showing up in conversations, someone genuinely unsure who owns a decision that used to have an obvious owner by default.

The mistake I watched happen, and had to correct for, in our own growth was building some of that infrastructure reactively, after the confusion had already cost real time and a few genuinely avoidable mistakes, rather than slightly ahead of the curve. Since then, I've tried to build a habit of asking, at every stage, what specific piece of infrastructure the next headcount milestone will require, and building it while the current size still makes it feel slightly premature, rather than waiting until the gap becomes obviously painful.

Leading our US expansion more recently, HR, legal, banking, insurance, tax, entity setup, required applying that same instinct to a market I hadn't built infrastructure in before. The specific playbook changes country to country. The underlying discipline, building slightly ahead of the actual need rather than reactively behind it, has stayed exactly the same.

name: Jesse Newton
body:
As Xelix grew, individual teams started adopting AI tools on their own initiative, which is a genuinely healthy sign of a curious, capable team. It also produced a specific problem that's easy to underestimate until you're the person responsible for the whole operation: five different teams solving similar problems with five different tools, none of them talking to each other about what actually worked, some of them introducing real governance and data-handling risk nobody outside that specific team had visibility into.

Establishing an AI Centre of Excellence wasn't about slowing that experimentation down or centralizing every decision through one bottleneck. It was about building a shared place where a team's actual learning, this specific tool handled our use case well, this other one created a data-handling risk we didn't initially catch, could reach the rest of the company before another team quietly repeated the same mistake independently.

The hardest part of building this wasn't the governance framework itself, which is mostly a straightforward documentation exercise once you sit down to write it. It was convincing teams that had been experimenting successfully on their own that sharing their approach through a central function wouldn't slow them down, that it was genuinely there to help other teams learn faster, not to impose a slower, more bureaucratic process on the ones already moving well.

What's actually validated the approach, months in, is a specific pattern: a team building something new now checks the Centre of Excellence's shared learnings before starting from scratch, and more than once that's saved real weeks that would otherwise have gone into rediscovering a data-handling issue another team had already quietly solved. That's the actual test of whether a central function like this earns its place. Not whether it exists on an org chart, but whether teams genuinely choose to use it before building something themselves.

name: Jesse Newton
body:
I recently completed my Chartered Governance Institute qualification, studying governance formally alongside years of actually doing operations work in practice. Doing the formal study after already having the practical experience, rather than before, gave me a specific perspective I don't think I'd have gotten doing it the other way around.

Much of what the formal qualification covers, board structure, decision rights, accountability frameworks, I'd already been building intuitively at Xelix through the OKR cadence and the operating systems I'd put in place scaling the company. Studying the formal theory afterward mostly confirmed that the instincts I'd built through direct experience were sound, which was reassuring, but the genuinely useful part was different: the qualification gave me language and structure for governance gaps I'd been sensing intuitively but hadn't fully named or systematized yet.

A specific example: I'd long felt that our decision rights around certain cross-functional calls were slightly unclear, without being able to articulate exactly what was wrong beyond a vague sense that meetings sometimes ended without a clear owner walking away with the actual call to make. The formal governance framework gave me precise language for that gap, decision rights versus decision input, and a structured way to actually fix it rather than just sensing something was off without a clear next step.

What I'd tell any operations leader considering formal governance training after they already have real practical experience is that the value isn't learning something entirely new. It's getting precise language and structure for problems you've likely already sensed intuitively, which turns a vague discomfort into something you can actually name, diagnose, and fix directly, rather than working around it indefinitely without quite being able to explain what's wrong.

name: Paris Haig
body:
Before enterprise SaaS, I sold Lo Bros Kombucha, Bootleg Booch, and plant-based milk for a company called Soulfresh, building relationships and winning new business across online and wholesale grocery channels. Going from consumer beverage sales to leading account management for enterprise finance software looks, on the surface, like two unrelated careers.

What actually transferred, and what I didn't fully appreciate until years into enterprise SaaS, was a specific instinct built from selling a product where the buyer had genuinely infinite alternatives sitting on the same shelf. A grocery buyer deciding whether to stock kombucha from us or a dozen nearly identical competitors makes that decision based almost entirely on the relationship and the specific, concrete case for why this particular brand deserves shelf space this particular quarter. There's no elaborate ROI model to lean on. There's just whether the relationship and the pitch are genuinely strong enough to earn a decision that could easily go a different way.

Enterprise account management, by comparison, often has more structural advantages built in, a signed contract, a working implementation, genuine switching costs for the customer. It's tempting to let those structural advantages do more of the relationship work than they actually should, coasting on the fact that a customer probably won't churn easily rather than actively earning their continued trust the way I had to earn a grocery buyer's shelf space every single quarter with no guarantee it would still be there.

What consumer sales taught me that I still apply now is treating every account renewal conversation with the same urgency I'd have treated a grocery buyer's quarterly shelf reset, as though the relationship genuinely has to be re-earned, not assumed. Customers who feel that ongoing effort expand and stay. The ones who sense they're being coasted on, however strong the contract's switching costs, eventually find a reason to leave anyway.

name: Paris Haig
body:
Before joining Xelix, I led an Enterprise Customer Success team at Darktrace, a company selling into an even more anxiety-inducing category than finance software: cybersecurity, where a customer's fear isn't primarily about wasted spend but about a genuine breach happening on their watch. Leading account management now in accounts payable, I've noticed how much of what I learned there transfers to a category most people wouldn't immediately connect to cybersecurity.

Both categories share a specific customer psychology: the value of the product is most visible in the moment something bad almost happened and got caught, a threat detected before it caused damage, a duplicate payment or a fraud attempt flagged before it cleared. That's a genuinely harder value story to keep visible to a customer than a product whose value shows up in obvious, positive, easily-celebrated wins. A customer forgets, month to month, how much risk they're not experiencing precisely because the tool is working quietly in the background.

At Darktrace, we built a discipline of proactively surfacing exactly what had been caught and prevented, on a regular cadence, rather than waiting for a renewal conversation to remind a customer why the relationship mattered. I've built the same discipline into how our team runs account management here: a regular, specific accounting of what Xelix actually caught this quarter, framed not as a marketing update but as a genuine answer to a question every finance leader is quietly asking themselves, is this thing actually still earning its cost.

The lesson that transferred most directly from cybersecurity to finance software is that prevention-based value needs to be actively narrated, regularly and specifically, or a customer's memory of it fades faster than the actual risk it's preventing ever does.

name: Paris Haig
body:
A lot of account expansion strategy in enterprise SaaS gets framed around upselling, identifying a feature the customer doesn't currently use and building a pitch for why they should add it. Leading account management for global enterprise customers, I've come to think that framing gets expansion conversations backwards more often than it gets them right.

The expansion conversations that actually land well don't start with a feature we want to sell. They start with a specific problem the customer is already experiencing that we happen to already have a solution for sitting unused in their existing contract. A finance team struggling with vendor master data quality, mentioning it almost in passing during an unrelated check-in call, is a considerably stronger expansion opportunity than a scheduled pitch for our Vendors module built around a feature list rather than a problem the customer actually named themselves.

That distinction changes how I train our account managers to run regular customer conversations. Instead of a quarterly business review built around what we want to present, we're listening specifically for the problem the customer names unprompted, the thing genuinely bothering them this month, and only then checking whether something already in our platform solves it. The pitch that follows isn't a sales pitch at that point. It's simply pointing out that a problem they already named has an answer they're already paying for but haven't turned on yet.

Expansion revenue built this way tends to feel, to the customer, less like being sold to and more like being genuinely helped, which matters enormously for retention beyond the immediate expansion itself. A customer who expanded because we solved a problem they named trusts the next conversation considerably more than one who expanded because a quarterly pitch deck made a compelling case for a feature they hadn't been actively missing.

name: Grant Marshall
body:
I spent eleven years at Zuora, starting as an Enterprise Business Representative and working through Account Executive, Strategic Account Executive, and eventually Regional Vice President of EMEA Growth. Eleven years is long enough that people reasonably ask what finally made me leave, and the honest answer isn't dissatisfaction with Zuora. It's that I'd run out of genuinely new versions of the job to grow into there.

Each promotion at Zuora had given me a real, meaningfully different challenge, new territory, more complex deals, eventually a whole region's growth strategy to own. By the RVP role, I'd built and rebuilt that muscle across UK, Northern Europe, Benelux, the Nordics, and Israel. The role kept expanding geographically without changing in kind, and I noticed I was solving increasingly similar problems across new markets rather than solving a genuinely new class of problem the way each earlier promotion had offered.

Joining Xelix as Head of Sales for Mid Market is a different kind of challenge than another region at a mature, subscription-billing category leader. It's building a go-to-market motion for a specific segment at a company still actively defining its playbook, in a category, accounts payable automation, that Zuora's billing world only touches at the edges. That's the genuinely new problem I'd stopped finding inside Zuora's structure, however much room the company still had to grow.

Eleven years somewhere isn't a lack of ambition if the role keeps handing you a real, different problem each time. It becomes worth leaving once the problems start rhyming with ones you've already solved, and recognizing that specific shift, rather than leaving on a fixed schedule or staying out of pure comfort, is the actual judgment call worth getting right.

name: Grant Marshall
body:
Zuora sells subscription billing and monetization software, a genuinely different product category than Xelix's accounts payable controls. Making the jump, I expected to need to relearn most of my sales approach from scratch. What's actually transferred, more than I expected, is a specific instinct about how finance buyers evaluate risk versus how they evaluate opportunity, regardless of which specific finance function is being sold into.

Selling billing software at Zuora, the buyer's excitement was usually opportunity-led: new revenue models Zuora's platform would let them launch, subscription structures they couldn't easily support with their current billing stack. The sale was largely about launching something new the finance and product teams wanted to do but currently couldn't. Selling AP controls at Xelix, the buyer's motivation is almost entirely risk-led: preventing a loss that's already quietly happening, not enabling a new capability they're excited to launch.

That distinction changes the entire emotional register of a sales conversation, and it took me longer to adjust to than I expected given how much of the underlying sales mechanics, stakeholder mapping, procurement navigation, multi-threading a deal, stayed genuinely similar across both categories. An opportunity-led buyer wants to feel excited about a future state. A risk-led buyer wants to feel reassured that a present, ongoing cost is actually being addressed, and excitement-oriented sales language, applied to that second kind of buyer, tends to read as slightly tone-deaf to what they're actually anxious about.

What's carried over cleanly regardless of category is the discipline of multi-threading a deal early, making sure a decision doesn't rest entirely on one champion who could leave or lose influence mid-cycle. What's had to be genuinely rebuilt is the emotional register of the pitch itself, moving from selling opportunity to selling reassurance against a cost the buyer already knows, somewhere, they're currently absorbing.

name: Grant Marshall
body:
Coming from eleven years largely focused on enterprise accounts at Zuora, taking on Head of Sales for Mid Market at Xelix surprised a few former colleagues, who assumed it was a step down in complexity or ambition. I've found the opposite to be closer to true, and it's changed my view of where the actually interesting sales problems in this category currently sit.

Enterprise deals, for all their size and prestige, often follow a fairly well-worn procurement path once you've run enough of them: security review, legal negotiation, a predictable sequence of stakeholders who've bought enterprise software before and know the dance. Mid-market finance teams evaluating AP automation for the first time are frequently doing so without that same institutional experience, which means the sales conversation has to do more genuine education, and the buyer's actual decision criteria are less standardized and more specific to their own particular situation.

That lack of a well-worn path makes mid-market selling considerably harder to run at pure volume with a scripted playbook, and considerably more interesting to actually think through deal by deal. A mid-market finance leader evaluating us for the first time needs a genuinely different conversation than the fifth enterprise CFO I'd talk to in a quarter who already has a mental model for how a vendor evaluation goes.

I'd rather build a genuinely thoughtful mid-market motion, one that treats each prospect's specific situation seriously rather than running a fast, standardized enterprise playbook at a smaller scale, than assume mid-market is simply a lower-stakes, lower-complexity version of the enterprise sale I already know well. The size of the deal is smaller. The actual sales problem, in my experience so far, is not.

name: Jim McCoy
body:
In 2014, I was managing security tools and operations at Facebook when Heartbleed hit, a vulnerability in OpenSSL that quietly exposed encryption keys across an enormous share of the internet. I was one of the people directly involved in the company's response, and the specific thing that stayed with me wasn't the technical fix itself. It was how differently the crisis felt from the inside compared to how it read in the press afterward.

From outside, Heartbleed read as a clean story: vulnerability discovered, patched, certificates rotated, crisis over. From inside, the actual work was considerably messier and less linear, figuring out which systems were genuinely exposed versus theoretically exposed, which certificates needed emergency rotation versus could wait for a scheduled cycle, all while genuinely not knowing yet how bad the exposure actually was, because the vulnerability had existed silently for roughly two years before anyone found it.

That gap, between the clean narrative a crisis becomes afterward and the genuinely uncertain, incomplete-information reality of actually living through it, is the thing I now watch for in every security incident I've managed since, including the ones I've led directly at Auros and in my own company, Q-Branch Labs. The postmortem always reads cleaner than the incident felt. That's not dishonesty. It's just how narrative works once the uncertainty has resolved and you know how the story ends.

What I try to build into every team I lead now is comfort with that uncertain middle, the part where you genuinely don't yet know the scope of a problem and have to make real decisions anyway. Teams that only train on clean postmortems, without ever practicing the uncomfortable, uncertain middle, tend to freeze exactly when a real incident puts them there for the first time.

name: Jim McCoy
body:
After years managing security operations at Facebook, I founded Q-Branch Labs, building the Q-Branch Vektor, a piece of hardware designed to extend a company's corporate security perimeter into remote employees' home networks. I owned the entire system architecture, from on-device security to manufacturing and fulfillment, applying machine learning anomaly detection to network flow data to catch malware and attacks before they reached a corporate network.

The idea came directly from a gap I kept seeing at Facebook: a company can secure its own office network thoroughly, and that security effectively stops the moment an employee works from home on a consumer-grade router with no real protection behind it. Building hardware to close that gap was a genuinely hard problem, harder than the software security work I'd done before, because hardware forces you to solve manufacturing, fulfillment, and physical logistics alongside the actual security engineering, with none of software's easy ability to patch a mistake remotely after the fact.

I ran that company for five years, through real technical wins, the anomaly detection genuinely worked well against real attack patterns in production. What eventually pulled me back toward operating inside larger organizations, first at Auros and now at Xelix, was recognizing that hardware security at the scale a company like Q-Branch would have needed to reach required a kind of sustained capital and go-to-market apparatus that a small, technically-founded team genuinely struggles to build alongside the actual engineering.

I don't regret the five years, and the anomaly detection approach we built there directly shapes how I approach infrastructure security now, at considerably larger scale. What I learned, plainly, is that a genuinely good technical solution to a real gap doesn't automatically solve the separate, equally hard problem of building the business apparatus around it.

name: Jim McCoy
body:
At Auros, I led DevOps and infrastructure for a globally distributed cryptocurrency fintech running high-frequency trading and automated market-making, through a period the team tripled in size, thirty to over a hundred fifty people. Part of that work involved building an encrypted execution environment for secure DeFi wallet operations using AWS Nitro Enclaves, a technology most engineering leaders outside crypto and fintech haven't had reason to work with directly.

Nitro Enclaves create an isolated compute environment where even someone with root access to the parent instance genuinely cannot see what's happening inside the enclave, which matters enormously when the thing running inside it controls real financial assets. Building that environment properly meant thinking about a threat model most infrastructure work doesn't have to seriously consider: not just external attackers, but the possibility that an internal actor, even one with legitimate elevated access, might need to be architecturally prevented from ever seeing certain operations, not just policy-prevented through access controls that a determined insider could work around.

That's a genuinely different security posture than most companies build toward, because it assumes a level of distrust in your own privileged access that feels uncomfortable to design for explicitly. Most infrastructure security reasonably assumes that someone with root access is trusted by definition. Building for a threat model where that assumption doesn't fully hold, because the stakes of a single compromised insider are existential rather than merely costly, changes nearly every architectural decision.

Moving into a role like Head of Platform Engineering at Xelix, where the sensitivity is financial control data rather than crypto custody specifically, that same instinct, question which of your own trust assumptions are load-bearing versus merely convenient, and design deliberately around the ones that genuinely can't afford to be wrong, has carried over directly, even though the specific technology stack looks nothing alike.

name: Aliya J.
body:
My background is ACA, a chartered accountant by training, before I ever moved into leading professional services and customer success functions. Fifteen years later, running Services and Support at Xelix, I still think that accounting foundation shapes how I lead differently than most services leaders whose background is purely operational or consulting.

Accounting training builds a specific discipline: the number has to actually reconcile, and if it doesn't, the problem isn't cosmetic, it's real, and it needs finding regardless of how inconvenient the timing is. I've carried that discipline directly into how I run a services organization. When a customer's implementation timeline slips, or a CSAT score drops in a specific segment, my instinct isn't to explain it away with a narrative. It's to find the actual reconciling detail, the specific account, the specific week, the specific handoff that broke, the same way I'd have traced a discrepancy in a set of accounts years earlier.

That instinct has mattered enormously scaling our services function from three people to twenty over eighteen months, building an operating model running up to a hundred concurrent projects. At that scale, a services leader relying purely on general sentiment, things feel like they're going well, is flying without the specific data that actually tells you where the next problem is quietly forming before it becomes visible in a customer's overall satisfaction score.

I don't think every services leader needs a formal accounting background to build that discipline. I do think the instinct itself, treating every metric as something that has to genuinely reconcile against reality rather than a rough vibe check, is the actual differentiator between a services function that scales cleanly and one that discovers its problems only once a customer's already frustrated enough to escalate.

name: Aliya J.
body:
Leading Services and Support at Xelix, I scaled the function from three people to twenty in eighteen months, building an operating model that now runs up to a hundred concurrent implementation projects while maintaining a 4.8 customer satisfaction score. Growth at that pace forces a specific set of decisions that a smaller, slower-growing team can genuinely defer, and I want to name the ones that mattered most rather than describe the growth in the abstract.

The first was pricing methodology. At three people, services can run informally, scoped project by project based on whoever's available and however much time it seems to need. At twenty people running a hundred concurrent projects, that informality becomes a genuine liability, because inconsistent scoping produces inconsistent delivery timelines, and inconsistent timelines are what actually erode a 4.8 CSAT score faster than almost anything else. Building real, repeatable pricing and delivery playbooks was the unglamorous foundation everything else depended on.

The second was reducing implementation resets, projects that had to restart partway through because scoping or expectations were wrong from the start. We cut those by ninety five percent, and the fix wasn't better project management in the moment. It was catching scoping mismatches earlier, before a project ever formally kicked off, which meant investing real time in a more rigorous pre-sales-to-delivery handoff than felt necessary back when the team was small enough that everyone naturally stayed in sync informally.

The third, and the one I'd underestimated most going in, was that scaling internationally, building our market entry into India specifically, required a genuinely different delivery model, a follow-the-sun structure, rather than simply replicating the UK team's approach at a larger scale in a new location. Growth at this pace rarely rewards doing more of what worked before. It rewards recognizing early which parts of what worked before were specific to the smaller scale and won't actually survive the jump.

name: Aliya J.
body:
I'm currently building the internal case for a dedicated Services P&L at Xelix, treating professional services as its own accountable business line rather than a cost center supporting the product sale. It's a harder internal argument than it might sound, and I want to explain why, because I don't think the resistance to it is unreasonable, even though I believe the case is right.

The natural objection to a Services P&L is that services exists to support successful product adoption, not to generate its own margin, and turning it into a standalone financial line risks optimizing services delivery for profitability in ways that could quietly work against the customer's actual best interest. That's a legitimate concern, and I've had to build the case carefully enough to address it directly rather than dismiss it.

What's actually convinced skeptical stakeholders, more than any abstract argument about services maturity, is showing the specific decisions a Services P&L would force that currently get made without adequate financial rigor: whether to staff a complex enterprise implementation with senior consultants at real cost, or whether pricing for a specific segment of customers is actually covering the true cost of the delivery model those customers require. Without a dedicated P&L, those decisions get made informally, often erring toward under-resourcing because the cost isn't visible against a dedicated budget the way it would be under real financial accountability.

The argument I keep making isn't that Services should chase margin at the expense of customer outcomes. It's that financial accountability and customer outcomes aren't actually in tension the way the initial objection assumes, and that a function without its own P&L tends to under-invest in exactly the resourcing that would improve both delivery quality and margin simultaneously, simply because nobody's forced to look at the true cost clearly enough to make that case internally.

name: Luciana Juarez
body:
I joined Xelix after cold-messaging CEO Paul Roiter directly on LinkedIn, following the news of the company's Series B raise. No warm introduction, no recruiter reaching out first. I saw the funding news, had a genuine read on why this specific moment mattered for a sales development leader, and messaged him directly rather than waiting to see if a role would eventually get posted somewhere.

I'd spent over a decade in international and local SDR and BDR leadership by that point, across music, fitness, HR tech, and sales tech, and I'd learned something about hiring timing that most job seekers underweight: the best roles at a growing company often don't exist yet in a formal job posting at the exact moment they'd benefit most from being filled. A fresh funding round is one of the clearest public signals that a company is about to need exactly the kind of function I build, and waiting for the posting to appear means competing with everyone else who saw the same news and had the same idea slightly later.

The message itself wasn't a generic congratulations. It named something specific about the stage Xelix was clearly entering, the scaling problem a Series B company moving upmarket typically hits in its outbound motion, and made a direct, specific case for why that problem was exactly the one I'd spent a decade solving elsewhere. Paul told me later that specificity, not the boldness of messaging a CEO directly, was what actually got a reply.

I now lead a sixteen-person SDR team here. The lesson I'd pass on to anyone eyeing a company's news for a similar opening isn't send more cold messages. It's that a message naming the specific problem a public moment creates, rather than a generic expression of interest, is what actually earns a real response from someone busy enough to ignore nearly everything else in their inbox that week.

name: Luciana Juarez
body:
Leading sales development, I use MEDDPICC, BANT, and Sandler, three genuinely different qualification methodologies, depending on the specific deal and buyer in front of the team, rather than standardizing our entire process around a single one, which is what most sales leadership advice would tell you to do for the sake of consistency.

BANT works well for a straightforward, lower-complexity deal where budget, authority, need, and timeline are the actual variables that determine whether a deal is real. It's fast and it doesn't over-engineer a qualification conversation that genuinely doesn't need more structure than that. MEDDPICC earns its place in a genuinely complex enterprise deal, where multiple stakeholders, a formal decision process, and real competitive pressure make a simpler framework miss real risk sitting inside a deal that looks qualified on the surface. Sandler's approach to genuinely uncovering pain, rather than just confirming a prospect fits a checklist, matters most in a category like ours, where a finance leader may not have fully quantified the problem themselves yet, and a purely checklist-driven qualification conversation would miss that unquantified pain entirely.

The discipline this actually requires from a team isn't picking a framework and following it faithfully. It's training reps to correctly diagnose, within the first few minutes of a conversation, which kind of deal they're actually in, then applying the framework built for that specific situation rather than forcing every conversation through the same structure regardless of fit.

That's a harder skill to train than simply teaching one methodology thoroughly, and it's slower to onboard a new SDR against. It's also produced a team that qualifies more accurately across a genuinely varied set of deal types than a team drilled on a single framework applied uniformly ever could, because the actual variable determining deal quality was never the framework. It was always whether the framework matched what that specific conversation actually needed.

name: Luciana Juarez
body:
Before enterprise sales development, I worked in business development at Sony Music Entertainment in Buenos Aires, and before B2B tech more broadly, I spent time in artist and repertoire scouting and business development in the music industry. The jump from music to enterprise SaaS pipeline management looks, on paper, like two unrelated careers, and in most ways it genuinely is.

What transferred more directly than I expected was a specific discipline the music industry teaches early and unforgivingly: most bets don't pay off, and the actual skill isn't avoiding that fact, it's building a pipeline wide enough, and honest enough in its own probability weighting, that the ones that do pay off cover for the ones that don't. Scouting talent means genuinely believing in every artist you sign while knowing, at the portfolio level, that most signings won't become the breakout success the initial belief implied. Enterprise sales pipeline works the same way, structurally, even though the emotional register of the work is completely different.

What I've carried directly from that earlier career into how I coach SDRs now is a specific resistance to false precision in pipeline forecasting. A rep confident that a specific deal will close is providing useful information about their own read on that deal, not a guarantee, the same way an A&R scout's genuine conviction about an artist was never a guarantee of a hit record. Building a forecasting culture that respects a rep's conviction as real signal, without treating it as certainty, is the same discipline the music industry beat into me from a completely different starting point.

Moving between industries this different taught me that the specific domain knowledge resets completely each time. The actual discipline underneath managing a portfolio of uncertain bets, whether the portfolio is artists or enterprise deals, turned out to be the one thing that traveled cleanly the whole way.
